items.title: I get Fable-6 Level performance with this Workflow..
items.summary:

PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode

In this video, I'll show why agents grading their own work led me to build Council into PandaCode. I'll walk through the settings, reviewer lenses, and rules that send work back for fixes when the lowest score falls below the target. I'll follow the skill manager through its review rounds, explain how to give reviewers concrete UI goals, and share findings from security, release, and factual accuracy reviews. I'll cover the extra plan usage, diminishing returns, and mixed-model advice before explaining why the score still leaves taste and the final decision with you.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧠 Separate reviewers can challenge the self-assessment of agents that built the work.
🎯 Council lets you set a target score, a round limit, and the number of reviewers.
👥 Each reviewer gets a lens, and the lowest score counts rather than the average.

items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, PandaCode got a new feature a few days ago called Council, and I think it is the most useful thing I have added to it so far. I want to show you how it works and how I have been using it, but I also want to talk about why it works because the idea behind it is much older than any of these models. The idea is this. The one who makes a thing is the worst one to judge it. That is not an insult to the maker. It is just how making works. When you build something, you know what you meant to build and you see that intention every time you look at the result. A reviewer doesn't have your intention. A reviewer only has what is actually there. That is why writers have editors, why papers have peer review, and why no court lets you be the judge in your own case. AI agents have the same problem and they have it worse. Ask an agent to build a settings page and at the end it tells you everything is done and everything works. It is not really lying to you. It is grading its own homework and it has every reason to like the answer. I have a real number for this. A while ago I had seven agents build seven scenes of a video and I asked each one to score its own scene. Every single one gave itself a nine out of 10. Then I had separate agents look at the same scenes with no context at all and they scored them between 5.5 and eight. That gap is the whole reason this feature exists. Before Council, I spent about 10 days closing that gap with a prompt. At the end of almost every task, I would type something like use a council of agents to score your work out of 10 and keep going until you reach a nine. I went back through my PandaCode logs and I had typed some version of that in 61 different tasks. And when you type the same paragraph 61 times, that paragraph wants to be a button. So, now it is a button. Let me show you. In PandaCode, inside the prompt box right next to the other toggles, there is a small-scale icon. If you click it, you get a little panel with one switch, three settings, and a box that starts new threads with Council on. The first is a target score, which is nine by and you can take it down to seven or all the way up to 10. The second is max rounds, which is 10 by default, and the third is the number of reviewers, which you can leave on auto so that the lead agent decides how many the work needs. Once you turn it on, Pandacode starts a team for that task if you didn't have one already. The lead agent plans the work and hands it to workers like it always does. The difference comes at the end because the lead is not allowed to just say that it is done anymore. Instead, it has to call a council. It picks the reviewers and it gives each one a lens. A lens is just the one thing that reviewer cares about. The first rule is that the lowest score counts and not the average. If two reviewers give you a 9.5 and the security reviewer gives you a six, then your score is six. An average lets a strong part hide a weak part, and nobody cares how good your design was on the day your tokens leaked. The second rule is that the reviewers never see the target and they never see the old scores. If a reviewer knows that you want a nine, you will get a nine. If it knows that the last round was a seven, it will hand you a polite eight. They get none of that. The third rule is that every round gets fresh reviewers, and this one matters more than it looks. If I review your work and you fix it and I look again, then I'm not really looking at your work anymore. I'm looking at the difference and I'm checking whether you did what I said. A fresh reviewer can't do that. It sees the thing the way a new user would see it, and that is the only view that counts. And the fourth rule is that the lenses are locked after round one. So the lead can't swap a strict reviewer for a friendlier one halfway through. All of this is enforced by the app itself and not by a prompt. If the lead tries to finish below the target, Pandacode refuses and tells it to fix the blockers and call a new round. Let's see a real one. I asked Pandacode to build a skill manager for itself and I said the UX had to be top notch. The workers built it and then the first council came back. You can see the strip at the top of the prompt box here. It shows the round and the lowest score next to the target. If I open it, there is one row for each reviewer and the lowest score of round one was a five. And the findings were not nitpicks. One reviewer found that switching projects did nothing for tasks that run in a work tree. Another found that some skills were shown as installed in about 14 tools, whether those tools were on my machine or not. And the third just said the scope switcher was misaligned in every screenshot. The lead sends workers to fix those, and then it calls three new reviewers, and it keeps doing that. The score went from five to six to seven, and then it stayed between six and seven for about 18 rounds. By round 22, it was at 8.5. And a reviewer still found that a failed uninstall could leave a skill half deleted with no way to undo it. That got fixed, and round 23 came back with a nine. It ended at the limit of 25 rounds with a nine. My target was 9.5. So the strip said it stopped at the round limit, and it handed the decision back to me. You get that same choice anytime the lead is stuck. You can keep fixing, you can lower the target, or you can press accept and finish. Once it is settled, each row shows the first score and the final score side by side. Now, if you want better UIs out of this, look at my prompt here. It just said top notch, and that is not a goal a reviewer can check. The reviewers can only score against the goal you give them and not against your taste. So say it in the prompt. Instead of top notch, I would now write the scope switcher lines up with the search field in every state, install, uninstall, and undo each take one click, and nothing moves when a list loads. Name the states too. Say empty loading error and a list of 200 skills because a reviewer only screenshots the states you name. The lead happened to pick a reviewer who took screenshots, and that one caught the switcher. Don't leave that to luck. Write that one reviewer must run the app and judge screenshots, not the code. And split the eye from the hands. One lens for how it looks and one for how it behaves when you click fast. So this is kind of great for UIs, but the thing that surprised me is how far you can take it because a lens can be anything on the phone app which can control panda code on your computer. The security lens found in round one that a phone with view only access could read the output of every terminal on the machine. I would not have found that by clicking around. When I redesigned how tool calls look in the chat, the reviewers didn't judge the mockups. They ran the new design against my real history and told me that about 4,200 old records now read as junk. On a release, I had one lens for release notes accuracy and another for build integrity. And the build lens caught that the commit I had tagged never actually passed CI. It works on things that aren't code as well. On a review script, the factual accuracy lens caught the voiceover saying $203 where the evidence said $23.04. On a thumbnail, there was a lens for click appeal and it pointed out that the thumbnail showed a different product than the video was about. My favorite ones are two lenses that the lead picked on its own called report honesty and diagnosis quality. An agent had told me a recording kept failing because my Mac was overloaded. The reviewer went and read the crash reports, said the explanation didn't hold up, and gave that diagnosis a three out of 10. It was not scoring the work there. It was scoring whether I was being told the truth. And yes, the council feature was built with a council. The score stalled at 7 to 8 for four rounds until one reviewer wrote that there was just too much machinery. So the next pass deleted code instead of adding it and the accept and finish button came out of that same council a few rounds later. Now, it's not perfect and I want to be honest about that. The first thing is the cost. In three days, my councils ran about 250 rounds with 837 reviewers and that is roughly 180 hours of agent time. The panel says it uses more of your plan and it means it. So it is not something I turn on for a typo fix. Second, not one of my councils with a 9.5 target has reached it yet. They usually start between five and seven and they end between eight and nine. In one task, a lens gave a six in round one and a six again in round 24. The skill manager got from five to seven in three rounds. Getting from seven to nine took 20 more. Most of those rounds moved the score very little, but round 22 found the uninstall bug. So, I leave the target at nine and the rounds at five or 10 for most work, and I only pay for 25 when losing someone's data is on the table. Third, reviewers do real work on your machine. Once, a reviewer filled my disk because it compiled the app to check its work. One more tip, mix your models. Three reviewers on this same model is really one opinion three times. If you have Panda Router on, it tries to give each reviewer a different model, and I would keep it that way. And that brings me back to the start. A score of nine is not the truth. It doesn't mean the work is good. It means a few strangers who each care about a different thing looked hard at it and could not find much to complain about. A score is not taste. Taste stays with you because you choose the goal, you set the bar, and you decide when to stop. What council changes is the question I used to ask, did the agent say that it's done? Now I ask, who else looked at it? And done stops being something that an agent says and becomes something that it has to earn. By the way, the frames of this video were scored by a council too. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. [music] If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
